title: Jack-o'-lantern
description: Carved pumpkin or root vegetable lantern
wiki_lead:
A jack-o'-lantern (or jack o'lantern) is a carved lantern, most commonly made from a pumpkin, or formerly a root vegetable such as a mangelwurzel, rutabaga or turnip. Jack-o'-lanterns are associated with the Halloween holiday. Its name comes from the phenomenon of strange lights flickering over peat bogs, called jack-o'-lanterns (also known as will-o'-the-wisps). It is suggested that the name also has ties to the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, a drunkard who, after deceiving people throughout his life and even Satan, is doomed to roam the Earth with only a hollowed turnip to light his way.
Jack-o'-lanterns carved from pumpkins are a yearly Halloween tradition that developed in the United States when Celtic influenced immigrants brought their root vegetable carving traditions with them.  It is common to see jack-o'-lanterns used as external and interior decorations prior to and on Halloween.
To make a jack-o'-lantern, the top of a pumpkin is cut off to form a lid, the inside flesh is scooped out, and an image—usually a "scary" or "funny" face—is carved out of the rind exposing the hollow interior. A light source, traditionally a candle flame or tealight, is placed within before the lid is closed. Artificial jack-o'-lanterns with electric lights are also marketed.

To make a jack-o'-lantern, the top of a pumpkin is cut off to form a lid, the inside flesh is scooped out, and an image—usually a "scary" or "funny" face—is carved out of the rind exposing the hollow interior. A light source, traditionally a candle flame or tealight, is placed within before the lid is closed. Artificial jack-o'-lanterns with electric lights are also marketed.


Etymology
The term jack-o'-lantern was originally used to describe the visual phenomenon ignis fatuus (lit., "foolish fire") known as a will-o'-the-wisp in English folklore. Used especially in East England, its earliest known use dates to the 1660s. The Oxford English Dictionary (OED) records use of the term in Britain from 1658 in reference to ignis fatuus, and from 1663 to 1704 in reference to a man with a lantern or to a night watchman. The OED gives 1837 as the earliest date for when the term was used to refer to a lantern carved from a turnip or pumpkin. 


History


Origin

The carving of vegetables has been a common practice in many parts of the world. It is believed that the custom of making jack-o'-lanterns at Halloween time began in Ireland and Britain. The tradition may have originated with ancient Celtic head veneration practices, where warriors would take the heads of defeated foes. These heads could be displayed for spiritual protection and were said to speak warnings. In the Táin Bó Cúailnge, a story from the Ulster Cycle, the severed head of Súaltam warns Cú Chulainn of the approaching Connacht army at the story's climax.
In the 19th century, "turnips or mangel wurzels, hollowed out to act as lanterns and often carved with grotesque faces," were used on Halloween in parts of England, Ireland, Wales and Scotland. In Gaelic-speaking regions, Halloween was also the festival of Samhain and was seen as a time when supernatural beings (the Aos Sí) walked the earth. In Wales such nights were known as Ysbrydnosau (spirit nights), with Calan Gaeaf being the one which occurred on the night of 31 October. grok_lead: A jack-o'-lantern is a carved lantern traditionally made from a hollowed-out pumpkin, turnip, or other vegetable, featuring a face or grotesque design illuminated from within by a candle or light source to create a glowing effect, and it serves as an iconic symbol of Halloween celebrations, particularly in the United States and Canada. The tradition originates from ancient Celtic folklore in Ireland and Scotland, where it is rooted in the festival of Samhain, a Gaelic harvest celebration marking the end of summer and the beginning of the darker half of the year, during which the boundary between the living world and the spirit realm was believed to thin, allowing supernatural beings to roam freely. In pre-industrial rural Ireland as early as the 1600s, people carved faces into turnips, potatoes, rutabagas, or beets and placed a lit coal or candle inside to ward off evil spirits, including restless souls like that of the legendary figure known as Stingy Jack. The core legend of Stingy Jack, a traditional Irish folktale originating in the 17th century, recounts a miserly blacksmith who repeatedly tricked the Devil into avoiding his soul's damnation, only to be barred from both Heaven and Hell upon his death; the Devil then granted him a single burning ember from Hell, which Jack carried in a carved-out turnip to light his eternal wanderings through the darkness, inspiring locals to create similar lanterns to frighten away his spirit and other malevolent entities on All Hallows' Eve. The term "jack-o'-lantern" derives from this story, evolving from phrases like "Jack of the Lantern" or references to will-o'-the-wisps (ignis fatuus), ethereal lights in marshes sometimes associated with lost souls. Irish immigrants brought the custom to North America during the mid-19th century, particularly amid the Great Potato Famine of the 1840s, where the abundance and larger size of native pumpkinsâintroduced to Europeans by Indigenous peoples as early as the 1600sâmade them a practical substitute for turnips, which were harder to carve and less readily available. By the late 19th century, pumpkin jack-o'-lanterns had become a staple of American Halloween observances, evolving from protective talismans into decorative elements for porches and parties, with early references appearing in print by the 1830s and widespread popularity by the early 20th century. Today, the practice persists globally, often incorporating modern variations like LED lights or elaborate designs, while retaining its ties to themes of harvest, mischief, and the supernatural.
